items.name: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 + Drugs Rules, 1945 (rule 106, Schedule J) + Cosmetics Rules, 2020 (rule 36): what drug and cosmetic labels, ads and listings may not claim
items.one_line: No drug may claim to prevent or cure any of the 51 Schedule J conditions (diabetes, cancer, obesity, baldness, fairness of the skin, height, memory, sexual performance and more); no cosmetic may convey a false or misleading idea, and a product making a drug claim is not a cosmetic at all.

sources.title: CDSCO: The Drugs Rules, 1945, compiled version as amended vide G.S.R. 360(E) dated 01-07-2024
sources.supports: rule 106(1) and 106(2) text; Schedule J list of 51 diseases and ailments; disclaimer that it is a compilation and that Ayush drug rules are published by the Ministry of Ayush

sources.title: CDSCO: The Cosmetics Rules, 2020
sources.supports: rule 36 (prohibition against false or misleading claims); rule 34 (manner of labelling); rule 37 hair-dye caution legend; rule 38 fluoride toothpaste

sources.title: CDSCO: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945 (as amended up to 31 Dec 2016)
sources.supports: Act s.3(aaa) definition of cosmetic; s.17 misbranded drugs; s.17C misbranded cosmetics; s.33E misbranded Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drugs

sources.title: CDSCO: Frequently Asked Questions on cosmetics (Q.54)
sources.supports: a product with a drug claim on its label or literature cannot be registered as a cosmetic

items.note: In force. Read 2026-10-13 in CDSCO's own PDFs: the Drugs Rules in CDSCO's compiled version (amended to G.S.R. 360(E) of 1 Jul 2024; CDSCO says it is a compilation, not the gazette), the Cosmetics Rules, 2020 as notified (later amendments not checked), and the Act in CDSCO's compilation to 31 Dec 2016. Penalties were not read, so none are stated. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Drugs Rules rule 106(1): no drug may claim to prevent or cure a Schedule J disease, nor 'convey to the intending user thereof any idea that it may prevent or cure' one. 'Convey any idea' catches implied claims, before-and-after visuals and testimonials, not only the words 'cures'. (2) Schedule J (51 entries) includes AIDS, cancer, diabetes, high/low blood pressure, obesity, baldness, change in colour of the hair and growth of new hair, premature greying of hair, fairness of the skin, premature ageing, power to rejuvenate, improvement in height of children/adults, increase in brain capacity and improvement of memory, improvement in vision, jaundice/hepatitis/liver disorders, piles and fistulae, kidney and gall-bladder stones, sexual impotence and sexual-performance claims, and form or structure of breast. (3) Rule 106(2): no drug may claim to procure or assist to procure miscarriage. (4) Act s.17(c) (and s.33E(c) for Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drugs): a drug is misbranded if its label, container 'or anything accompanying the drug' makes 'any false claim for the drug' or is 'false or misleading in any particular'. (5) Cosmetics Rules rule 36: 'No cosmetic may purport or claim to purport or convey any idea which is false or misleading to the intending user'; Act s.17C(c) makes a cosmetic misbranded for a false or misleading statement on the label or 'anything accompanying' it. (6) A cosmetic is defined by use for 'cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering the appearance' (Act s.3(aaa)); CDSCO FAQ Q.54: 'Products having drug claim do not come under the definition of cosmetic', so 'treats acne', 'cures dandruff' or 'heals' copy on a cosmetic is a drug claim. (7) Labels must carry the rule 34 particulars (name, manufacturer and address or 'Made in', expiry or use-before, batch number, manufacturing licence number, net contents, safety directions where a hazard exists); hair dyes need the rule 37 caution legend in English and local languages. Cross-reference comp:dmr_act_1954 (advertisement ban for listed diseases, any medium), comp:ayush_drug_advertisement_rule_170, comp:ucpmp_2024_pharma_promotion and comp:legal_metrology_packaged_commodities.

items.name: Ayush (Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani) drug advertisements: Drugs Rules rule 170, its 2024 omission and the Supreme Court orders of 2024-2025
items.one_line: Rule 170 required State approval (a Unique Identification Number) before any Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug ad and barred disease-cure claims; the Ministry of Ayush omitted it on 1 Jul 2024, the Supreme Court stayed that on 27 Aug 2024 and vacated the stay on 11 Aug 2025, so as read in Oct 2026 the rule stands omitted while the DMR Act, D&C Act misbranding and ASCI / CCPA rules still bite.

sources.title: Supreme Court of India, order of 11 Aug 2025 in W.P.(C) No. 645/2022 with W.P.(C) No. 400/2025 (digitally signed order; copy hosted by LiveLaw because the court's own servers refused connections on 2026-10-13)
sources.supports: the omission notification of 01.07.2024; text of the former Rule 170; extract of the 27.08.2024 stay order; disposal of the petition, liberty to challenge the omission, and vacation of the stay

sources.title: LiveLaw report, 11 Aug 2025 (secondary): Supreme Court vacates stay on Ayush Ministry's notification
sources.supports: secondary confirmation of the date and effect of the 11 Aug 2025 order

sources.title: CDSCO: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (compilation to 31 Dec 2016), s.33E
sources.supports: an Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug is misbranded if anything accompanying it makes a false claim or is false or misleading

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: OMITTED. The Supreme Court's order of 11 Aug 2025 records that the Ministry of Ayush notification of 01.07.2024 under the Drugs (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2024 'had omitted Rule 170'; on 27.08.2024 the Court had ordered that 'Rule 170 shall remain on the statute book and in force' till further orders; on 11 Aug 2025 it disposed of the petition, reserved liberty to parties with 'any grievance with regard to the omission of Rule 170' and said 'interim order dated 27.08.2024 stands vacated'. A later challenge in another forum is possible: check before telling a client the rule is gone for good. The order PDF was read in a copy hosted by LiveLaw (the court's own site refused connections today); the Ministry of Ayush gazette notification itself was not read. Rules for a copywriter: (1) The former Rule 170 (as extracted in the order) barred ASU drug ads 'for the use of diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention of any disease, disorder, syndrome or condition', and made other ads wait for a Unique Identification Number from the State Licensing Authority; with the omission, no State pre-approval number is needed, but the cure-claim limits below still apply. (2) The Drugs and Magic Remedies Act, 1954 still bars ads suggesting a drug for its scheduled diseases in any medium (comp:dmr_act_1954). (3) Act s.33E(c): an Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug is misbranded if anything accompanying it 'makes any false claim for the drug or which is false or misleading in any particular'. (4) The former Rule 170's rejection list is still a sound red-flag checklist (it mirrors DMR Act and ASCI risks): vulgarity or obscenity, sexual-organ or sexual-performance enhancement claims, 'photographs or testimonials of celebrities or government officials', references to a government body, a false impression of the drug's true character, and 'a misleading or exaggerated claim about the effectiveness'. (5) The ASCI Code and the CCPA 2022 guidelines apply to every ad regardless (comp:asci_code, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022).

items.name: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 Advertisement Code (Fifth Schedule) + Master Circular for Mutual Funds (20 Mar 2026) + AMFI rules for mutual fund distributors' communication
items.one_line: Every mutual fund ad or communication that may influence an investment decision carries the unchanged 14-word standard warning, no celebrities, no testimonials or rankings, no projections, and performance only in SEBI's fixed format; distributors (MFDs) show name, ARN and the 'AMFI-registered Mutual Fund Distributor' tagline, use only AMC-made scheme material and never indicate returns.

sources.title: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026, amended up to July 7, 2026: reg 2(c), reg 28 and Fifth Schedule (Advertisement Code)
sources.supports: definition of advertisement; Advertisement Code clauses (a)-(k) incl. standard warning wording, vernacular and audio-visual rules, no celebrities, no testimonials or rankings

sources.title: SEBI Master Circular for Mutual Funds, March 20, 2026 (HO/24/13/11(1)2026-IMD-POD-1/I/7602/2026), Chapter 14 Advertisements and para 21.13.5
sources.supports: performance-advertisement format (CAGR 1/3/5 years and since inception, Rs 10,000 point-to-point, regular vs direct plan, fund-manager disclosures, no past performance under six months); IDCW pay-out disclosure; Specialized Investment Fund standard warning

sources.title: AMFI Master Circular for Mutual Fund Distributors, AMFI/MFD-CIR/32/2025-26, January 14, 2026 (incl. Code of Conduct for MFDs)
sources.supports: mandatory tagline with name and ARN; no indicative or assured returns; AMC-supplied material only; no 'adviser' names unless SEBI-registered; no false statements on social media

sources.title: AMFI FAQs on Do's and Don'ts for MFDs (advertisements, websites, media channels; undated)
sources.supports: MFDs may advertise their services; no free-advice or free-portfolio-review lures; YouTube and social media: education only, no scheme-specific recommendations or performance claims, disclose MFD status and ARN

items.note: In force: the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 apply 'with effect from April 1, 2026' (text read as amended up to July 7, 2026); the Master Circular of March 20, 2026 replaced the one of June 27, 2024; AMFI's Master Circular for MFDs is dated January 14, 2026. All read 2026-10-13 on sebi.gov.in and amfiindia.com. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Scope: an advertisement is 'any communication issued by or on behalf of the mutual fund or asset management company that may influence the investment decision' (reg 2(c)), so social posts, reels, emails and creator scripts count. (2) Fifth Schedule: ads must be 'accurate, true, fair, clear, complete, unambiguous and concise'; no statements 'based on assumption/projections', no 'testimonials or any ranking based on any criteria', no exaggerated slogan inconsistent with the risk-return profile, 'No celebrities shall form part of the advertisement', no discrediting other ads or unfair comparisons. (3) Standard warning, word for word: 'Mutual Fund investments are subject to market risks, read all scheme related documents carefully.' No words added or removed; in the ad's own language for a vernacular ad; in audio-visual ads both shown and voiced, e.g. 'fourteen (14) words running for at least five (5) seconds'. (4) Performance ads (Master Circular ch. 14): CAGR for at least 1, 3 and 5 years and since inception, plus point-to-point returns on a Rs 10,000 investment, computed to the last month-end before the ad; say whether regular or direct plan; show the benchmark and the additional benchmark; add other schemes of the same fund manager; 'Where the scheme has been in existence for less than six months, past performance shall not be provided.' (5) A Specialized Investment Fund ad carries its own fixed warning (para 21.13.5), beginning 'Investments in Specialized Investment Fund involves relatively higher risk including potential loss of capital, liquidity risk and market volatility.' (6) Distributors (AMFI): show 'AMFI-registered Mutual Fund Distributor' with name and ARN (at least font size 12 in print, legible on websites, apps and all other communication); 'not provide any indicative portfolio or indicative yield or indicative return'; use AMC marketing material 'as is'; no 'Adviser', 'Wealth Manager' or 'Consultant' in the name unless SEBI-registered; on YouTube and social media, education only, no scheme-specific recommendations or performance claims, disclose MFD status and ARN; no 'free advise' or 'free portfolio review' lures (FAQ). Cross-reference comp:sebi_finfluencer_association and comp:asci_influencer.

items.name: SEBI advertisement code for Investment Advisers and Research Analysts (Master Circulars of February 6, 2026; first issued by circulars of April 2023)
items.one_line: Every ad or social post by a SEBI-registered investment adviser or research analyst shows the registered name, SEBI registration number, the fixed standard warning and disclaimers, gets prior approval from the supervisory body, and never promises assured, minimum or target returns, uses superlatives like 'Best' or 'No. 1', unverified past performance, misleading testimonials or the SEBI logo.

sources.title: SEBI Master Circular for Investment Advisers, HO/38/12/11(2)2026-MIRSD-POD/I/4300/2026, February 06, 2026, para 10 (Advertisement code and usage of brand name/trade name)
sources.supports: forms of communication covered; mandatory disclosures, standard warning and disclaimers; prohibitions (assured returns, superlatives, unverified past performance, free claims, SEBI logo); prior approval; five-year retention

sources.title: SEBI Master Circular for Research Analysts, HO/38/12/11(1)2026-MIRSD-POD/I/4360/2026, February 06, 2026 (advertisement code)
sources.supports: the same code for research analysts, with RA-specific disclaimer wording

items.note: In force; both master circulars dated February 06, 2026 (read 2026-10-13 on sebi.gov.in) carry the code first issued by circulars of April 05 and April 06, 2023 (IA footnote). Rules for a copywriter: (1) Scope: 'all forms of communications' by or on behalf of the IA or RA that may influence investment decisions, expressly including email, text messaging, messaging platforms, 'social media platforms', radio, TV and video. (2) Must show: name as registered with SEBI, registered office address, SEBI registration number, logo or brand name, CIN if any; on SMS, pop-ups and social media where these do not fit, a hyperlink to the official website that carries them. (3) Standard warning in at least 10-point font, word for word: 'Investment in securities market are subject to market risks. Read all the related documents carefully before investing'; in audio-visual ads shown and voiced, e.g. '20 words running for at least 10 seconds'; accurately translated in a non-English ad. Securities shown as examples need 'The securities quoted are for illustration only and are not recommendatory'. Ads and client communication carry the disclaimer that begins 'Registration granted by SEBI, enlistment with IAASB and certification from NISM' and ends 'in no way guarantee performance of the IA or provide any assurance of returns to investors' (the RA version names BSE and 'the intermediary'). (4) Banned: false, misleading, biased or deceptive statements 'based on assumptions or projections'; 'Any misleading or deceptive testimonials'; calling a report or service free unless it is free without condition; any promise of assured or risk-free return, and no implied 'minimum returns or target return or percentage accuracy'; discrediting other intermediaries; past performance or risk-return metrics unless verified by the Past Risk and Return Verification Agency (PaRRVA) and claimed as SEBI specifies; superlatives such as 'Best', 'No. 1', 'Top Adviser', 'Leading' (factual awards from independent organisations are allowed). (5) 'Advertisements shall not include SEBI Logo'; prior approval of the ad from the SEBI-recognised supervisory body; no games, leagues or competitions with prizes; a suspended IA or RA may not advertise; keep a copy of each ad for five years. Cross-reference comp:sebi_finfluencer_association (who a regulated entity may associate with) and comp:asci_influencer.

items.name: Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act, 2003 (COTPA) and COTPA Rules, 2004: tobacco advertising ban, indirect advertising, and health spots and warnings in films, TV and OTT
items.one_line: No one may take part in any ad that directly or indirectly promotes tobacco, or promote a tobacco brand in return for sponsorship; using a tobacco brand, its colours or smoking situations to sell anything else is indirect advertising; films, TV shows and OTT content showing tobacco must carry 30-second health spots, a static 'Tobacco kills'-type warning and a 20-second disclaimer, with no brand placement.

sources.title: MoHFW National Tobacco Control Programme: COTPA 2003, English version (scanned gazette copy)
sources.supports: s.3(a) definition of advertisement; s.5(1)-(3) ban on direct and indirect advertisement, point-of-sale and pack exceptions, sponsorship ban

sources.supports: rule 2(e) definition of indirect advertisement; rule 4 point-of-sale board limits; rule 4(7) masking of tobacco brands in media pictures and footage

sources.title: MoHFW: G.S.R. 708(E), COTPA Amendment Rules in force from 2 Oct 2012 (rules 7 and 8: old and new films and TV programmes)
sources.supports: health spots, static warning, audio-visual disclaimer, editorial justification, warning texts, language rule for films and TV

sources.title: MoHFW: G.S.R. 400(E), 31 May 2023, COTPA Amendment Rules, 2023 (rule 11: online curated content)
sources.supports: OTT health spots, static warning, disclaimer, language, ban on brand display and product placement, definition of online curated content (incl. podcasts)

items.note: In force. Read 2026-10-13 on the Health Ministry's NTCP site: the Act (Act 34 of 2003; scanned gazette copy, so wording below is copied with care from imperfect OCR), the 2005 amendment rules (G.S.R. 345(E)), the film and TV rules in force from 2 Oct 2012 (G.S.R. 708(E)) and the OTT rule notified 31 May 2023 (G.S.R. 400(E), in force three months after publication). The 2011 amendments (G.S.R. 619(E) and 786(E)) are image-only scans and were not read, so later changes to rule 4 may exist. India Code timed out today. Rules for a copywriter: (1) s.5(1): no tobacco producer or distributor may advertise, no one controlling a medium may carry a tobacco ad, and no person shall 'take part in any advertisement which directly or indirectly suggests or promotes the use or consumption' of tobacco, so the agency, writer and creator are covered. (2) 'Advertisement' includes any visible representation by notice, circular, label or wrapper and any announcement made orally or by light, sound, smoke or gas (s.3(a)). (3) s.5(3): no promotion of tobacco or of 'any trade mark or brand name' of tobacco in exchange for a sponsorship, gift, prize or scholarship. (4) Indirect advertisement (rule 2(e), 2005) covers: using a tobacco name or brand to market other goods, services and events; marketing tobacco under a brand known for other goods; using colours, layout or presentation associated with a tobacco product; and using tobacco products and smoking situations when advertising other goods and services. (5) The only advertising exceptions are on the pack itself and at the entrance or inside a shop selling tobacco (s.5(2) proviso); the 2005 rule 4 limits such a board to 60 cm by 45 cm with a warning 'Tobacco causes cancer' or 'Tobacco kills', and no brand pack shot, brand name or promotional message. (6) New films and TV programmes showing tobacco (rule 8, 2012) need an editorial justification to the CBFC, anti-tobacco health spots of at least thirty seconds at the beginning and middle, a static warning at the bottom of the screen while tobacco is shown, and an audio-visual disclaimer of at least twenty seconds at the beginning and middle, in the language of the film (or of its dub or subtitles); warnings are 'Smoking causes cancer' or 'Smoking kills' for smoking and 'Tobacco causes cancer' or 'Tobacco kills' for smokeless tobacco, black on white. (7) OTT (rule 11, 2023): a publisher of online curated content (which includes films, series, documentaries 'podcasts and other such content') showing tobacco must run the same spots, static warning and 20-second disclaimer in the content's language, and may not show 'the brands of cigarettes or other tobacco products or any form of tobacco product placement', or tobacco in promotional materials such as trailers. Cross-reference comp:surrogate_advertising_india, comp:cable_tv_advertising_code and comp:it_rules_2021_digital_news_code.

items.name: Surrogate and brand-extension advertising in India (alcohol, tobacco, betting): CCPA 2022 guideline 6, Cable TV Advertising Code brand-extension proviso, ASCI brand-extension qualification criteria and the 2024-2025 advisories
items.one_line: An ad for soda, music CDs, cards or a 'news' app that borrows a liquor, tobacco or betting brand's name, logo, colours, layout or situations to keep the banned product in view is a surrogate ad; a brand extension is lawful only if the ad shows only the real product, makes no reference to the banned one, and (for ASCI and TV) the extension passes turnover and spend-proportion tests.

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: CCPA guideline 6 in force since the 2022 notification; the Cable TV rule read as on 02.01.2025; ASCI criteria dated November 23rd, 2023; the CCPA (06 Mar 2024) and MIB (21 Mar 2024) advisories on betting are in force as advisories; the Health Ministry's March 2025 letter to the IPL is a request, not a rule. Press reports of draft CCPA rules on celebrity surrogate endorsements (late 2024) were not traced to any notification in this pass: do not cite them as law. Rules for a copywriter: (1) A surrogate advertisement is one for goods whose advertising is prohibited or restricted, made 'by circumventing such prohibition or restriction and portraying it to be an advertisement for other goods' (CCPA 2(h), 6(1)). (2) It is surrogate if it 'indicates or suggests directly or indirectly' the banned product, or 'uses any brand name, logo, colour, layout and presentation associated with' it (6(2)); the proviso saves 'mere use of a brand name or company name' shared with the banned product only if the ad is not otherwise objectionable. (3) On TV and cable, a brand-extension ad must show only the product advertised, make no direct or indirect reference to the prohibited product, contain no 'nuances or phrases promoting prohibited products', use no associated colours, layout or presentation and no 'situations typical for promotion of prohibited products'; the advertiser also needs a Chartered Accountant's certificate of real distribution and proportionate spend, an MIB finding of genuine brand extension and CBFC certification before telecast (rule 7(2)(viii)). (4) ASCI test: the extension is registered with an authority (GST, FDA, FSSAI, TM); a brand over two years old needs turnover above Rs 5 crore a year nationally or Rs 1 crore per state; a newer one needs one of Rs 20 lakh a month in sales, Rs 10 crore of exclusive fixed assets, long-term supply contracts, or turnover above 10% of the restricted brand's; the ad budget may not exceed 200% of the extension's sales in years 1 and 2, 100% in year 3, 50% in year 4 and 30% after; failing means 'a surrogate created to advertise a restricted category'. (5) Tobacco has its own indirect-advertising definition (comp:cotpa_tobacco_advertising). (6) Betting: the CCPA says celebrities and influencers promoting online betting are 'equally liable for participating in an illegal activity', and the MIB told influencers to refrain from promoting offshore betting 'including surrogate advertisements', with removal of posts or accounts as a consequence; online money games are covered by comp:online_gaming_act_2025. Cross-reference comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022, comp:cable_tv_advertising_code and comp:asci_code.

items.name: Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986
items.one_line: Criminal law: no one may publish, arrange or take part in any advertisement, or produce, sell or circulate any book, film, photograph, painting or figure, that depicts a woman's figure, form or body in a way that is indecent, derogatory to or denigrating women, or likely to deprave or corrupt public morality.
aliases: derogatory portrayal of women in ads

sources.title: Government of Tripura, Social Welfare department: text of the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986 (No. 60 of 1986) (state-government transcription; secondary to India Code)
sources.supports: s.2 definitions (advertisement, distribution, indecent representation of women); s.3 advertisement ban; s.4 publication ban and exceptions; s.6 penalty; s.7 offences by companies; s.8 cognizable and bailable

sources.title: India Code record for the Act (Act 60 of 1986; Ministry of Women and Child Development)
sources.supports: official record; the page returned HTTP 403 and timed out on 2026-10-13, so its text was not read

items.note: In force (central Act 60 of 1986). India Code refused the connection twice on 2026-10-13 (timeout, then HTTP 403), so the text was read in a Government of Tripura transcription, a secondary copy with small typing errors: confidence medium; check India Code before quoting a section in a legal document. Amendments after 1986 were not checked. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Definition (s.2): 'indecent representation of women' means depicting the figure of a woman, her form or body or any part of it so as to be 'indecent, or derogatory to, or denigrating women', or 'likely to deprave, corrupt or injure the public morality or morals'. (2) s.3: 'No person shall publish, or cause to be published, or arrange or take part in the publication or exhibition of' an advertisement containing it 'in any form': the brand, agency, copywriter, model, publisher and influencer are all within 'take part'. (3) 'Advertisement' includes any notice, circular, label, wrapper or other document and 'any visible representation made by means of any light, sound, smoke or gas', so packaging and labels count. (4) s.4 bans producing, selling, hiring out, distributing, circulating or posting any book, pamphlet, paper, slide, film, writing, drawing, painting, photograph, representation or figure containing it; exceptions are material justified as being for the public good in the interest of science, literature, art or learning, material kept or used bona fide for religious purposes, sculpture or paintings on ancient monuments or temples, and films governed by Part II of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (certified films are handled by the CBFC instead). (5) Penalty as printed in this copy (s.6): first conviction up to two years' imprisonment and fine up to two thousand rupees; second or later conviction six months to five years and fine of ten thousand to one lakh rupees; offences are cognizable and bailable (s.8); company officers in charge are liable unless they prove due diligence (s.7). Cross-reference comp:cable_tv_advertising_code (no derogatory image of women on TV) and comp:asci_code.

items.name: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 (as amended 2021 and by the Amendment Rules, 2026)
items.one_line: Every marketplace or inventory e-commerce listing must show the seller's details, total price in a single figure with its break-up, country of origin, return, refund, warranty, delivery and grievance information; sellers may not post reviews posing as consumers or misrepresent goods; from 1 January 2027 a price cut must show the 'prior price' (lowest price of the previous 30 days) and sponsored listings must be clearly labelled.

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: the 2020 Rules are in force since publication on 23 July 2020; the only 2021 amendment notified (G.S.R. 328(E), 17 May 2021) changed rule 4(1) on incorporation only; the June-July 2021 draft amendments (flash sales, mis-selling, cross-selling) were a consultation draft and are not listed among the notified instruments on the Department's page; the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) (Amendment) Rules, 2026 are dated 9 September 2026 and come into force from 1st January (the year digits did not extract from the official PDF; secondary reports say 1 January 2027). Until then the 2020 text applies. Rules for a copywriter writing listings, seller pages and sale banners: (1) Seller listings must show 'total price in single figure' with the break-up of compulsory and voluntary charges (delivery, handling, tax), the expiry date where applicable, country of origin, importer details for imports, grievance officer, and accurate exchange, return, refund (incl. (2) Fake reviews: no seller or inventory entity shall 'falsely represent itself as a consumer and post reviews' or misrepresent the quality or features of goods (rules 6(2), 7(2)); ads must be 'consistent with the actual characteristics, access and usage conditions' (rules 6(4)(c), 7(3)). (3) No price manipulation to impose an 'unjustified price' (rule 4(11)(a)); no consent recorded automatically, 'including in the form of pre-ticked checkboxes' (rule 4(9)); no cancellation charge unless the entity bears similar charges (rule 4(8)). (4) From the 2026 amendment: a price reduction must show the 'prior price', defined as 'the lowest price of a good or service thirty days prior to the announcement of price reduction'; sponsored listings must be 'distinctly identified with clear and prominent disclosures'; no misleading users 'by manipulating search result or search indexes'; marketplaces show seller name, address, customer care, ratings and the main ranking parameters in plain language; country of origin by its full name as under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules; the seller's name on the invoice in the same font size as the platform's; a yearly dark-pattern self-audit with a displayed certificate.
